# Integrability and the ensembles that replace thermal equilibrium {#sec-integrability}

An integrable quantum gas has interactions, collisions, entanglement growth, and
local relaxation. Its special feature is that collisions preserve much more
information than energy and particle number. Stable excitations retain their
rapidities, a momentum-like label, even after many encounters. The late-time local
state must remember their distribution.

This chapter builds that statement from wave functions to thermodynamics. We
use $\hbar=k_B=1$, $S^a=\sigma^a/2$, and natural logarithms. No Bethe ansatz
background is assumed. A *quasiparticle* is an excitation that propagates with a
well-defined label and energy over the scales of interest. In integrable models
it can remain stable indefinitely; in generic systems that stability is usually
approximate.

## What quantum integrability means operationally

There is no single definition that resolves every finite-dimensional quantum
model. Merely constructing all spectral projectors gives many commuting
operators for any Hamiltonian and does not explain local physics. The useful
many-body notion involves an extensive family of independent conserved
operators with sufficiently local densities, together with a scattering or
transfer-matrix structure that organizes them.

A local charge has the form $Q_r=\sum_xq_{r,x}$, with each density supported on
finitely many nearby sites. A *quasilocal* charge allows an expansion into
longer strings whose norms decay with support and whose total norm grows
extensively. Such charges constrain local states and can protect transport.
The familiar Hamiltonian is one member of the family. Integrability does not
mean that every observable is easy to calculate: overlaps, real-time correlation
functions, and finite-temperature dynamics can remain difficult.

In one-dimensional scattering, a characteristic property is *factorization*:
an $N$-particle collision can be resolved into two-particle collisions without
producing new sets of rapidities. Consistency requires different collision
orderings to agree, expressed by the Yang–Baxter equation when internal species
are present. This structure is restrictive. Generic three-body processes can
redistribute momenta while conserving total energy and momentum.

## Two magnons: constructing a Bethe wave function

Consider the XXZ chain with its fully polarized state as a reference, and
subtract the reference energy:

$$
H=J\sum_x\left[S_x^xS_{x+1}^x+S_x^yS_{x+1}^y+
\Delta(S_x^zS_{x+1}^z-1/4)\right].
$$

A down spin, called a magnon relative to this reference, hops with amplitude
$J/2$. A one-magnon plane wave has energy $J(\cos k-\Delta)$.
For two separated down spins at $x_1<x_2$, try

$$
\psi(x_1,x_2)=A_{12}e^{i(k_1x_1+k_2x_2)}+
A_{21}e^{i(k_2x_1+k_1x_2)}.
$$ {#eq-bethe-two-magnon}

The two terms allow the momenta to exchange. Away from contact, the lattice
Schrödinger equation gives
$E=J(\cos k_1+\cos k_2-2\Delta)$.
At adjacent sites, there are fewer allowed hops and a different interaction
energy. Comparing the adjacent equation to the extrapolated free equation
requires

$$
\psi(x,x)+\psi(x+1,x+1)=2\Delta\psi(x,x+1).
$$

The coincident amplitudes here are formal extensions of the plane-wave ansatz;
the spin Hilbert space still forbids two down spins on one site. Substitution
and cancellation of $e^{i(k_1+k_2)x}$ give

$$
\frac{A_{21}}{A_{12}}
=-\frac{1+e^{i(k_1+k_2)}-2\Delta e^{ik_2}}
{1+e^{i(k_1+k_2)}-2\Delta e^{ik_1}}.
$$ {#eq-bethe-scattering}

This ratio is the two-body scattering amplitude in the stated coefficient
convention. For real momenta it is a phase. At $\Delta=0$ it becomes $-1$,
as expected for the free-fermion representation. Complex momenta can describe
bound states; discarding them would omit physically important excitations.
Bethe's original construction [@bethe1931chain] is the ancestor of this method.

For many magnons, sum over all permutations of momenta and relate neighboring
permutation coefficients by this two-body amplitude. Periodic boundaries then
quantize momenta through accumulated propagation and scattering phases. The
result is an interacting quantization problem rather than independent free
standing waves.

## A continuum model with especially transparent thermodynamics

The repulsive Lieb–Liniger gas is convenient for deriving the thermodynamic
machinery. For $N$ bosons on a ring of length $L$, choose mass $m=1/2$:

$$
H=-\sum_{j=1}^N\partial_{x_j}^2+
2c\sum_{i<j}\delta(x_i-x_j),\qquad c>0.
$$ {#eq-bethe-ll}

The contact interaction imposes a derivative jump on the wave function at
$x_i=x_j$. In each ordered coordinate sector the wave function is a sum of
plane waves; the jump fixes their relative scattering phase. One convenient
logarithmic form of the periodic Bethe equations is

$$
Lk_j+\sum_{\ell\ne j}\theta(k_j-k_\ell)=2\pi I_j,
\quad
\theta(q)=2\arctan(q/c),
\quad
K(q)=\theta'(q)=\frac{2c}{c^2+q^2}.
$$ {#eq-bethe-quantization}

The quantum numbers $I_j$ are distinct integers or half-integers depending on
$N$ and the phase convention. Energies and momenta are
$E=\sum_jk_j^2$ and $P=\sum_jk_j$. The kernel $K$ is the derivative of a
collision phase; it measures how adding particles changes the density of allowed
rapidities. It is not a phenomenological relaxation rate.

## From discrete roots to a thermodynamic macrostate

In the thermodynamic limit, a microscopic list of roots is too detailed. Define
$\rho_p(k)dk$ as the number of occupied roots per unit physical length in
$[k,k+dk]$. Let $\rho_h$ count unoccupied available quantum numbers and
$\rho_s=\rho_p+\rho_h$ count all available states. The filling is
$\vartheta=\rho_p/\rho_s$.

Differentiate the counting function in @eq-bethe-quantization and replace the
root sum by an integral. The spacing of allowed quantum numbers gives

$$
2\pi\rho_s(k)=1+\int dq\,K(k-q)\rho_p(q).
$$ {#eq-bethe-root-density}

Thus interactions change the available density of states. A macrostate is
specified by the function $\rho_p$, or equivalently $\vartheta$, subject to
this equation. Its particle and energy densities are
$n=\int dk\,\rho_p(k)$ and $e=\int dk\,k^2\rho_p(k)$.
Infinitely many different functions can have the same $n$ and $e$.

To count microscopic realizations, divide rapidity space into small bins. A bin
contains $L\rho_sdk$ allowed quantum numbers and $L\rho_pdk$ occupied ones.
Its multiplicity is a binomial coefficient. Stirling's formula, followed by
summing bins, gives the Yang–Yang entropy density

$$
s_{\mathrm{YY}}=\int dk\,[\rho_s\ln\rho_s-\rho_p\ln\rho_p-
\rho_h\ln\rho_h]
=\int dk\,\rho_s\,h(\vartheta),
$$ {#eq-bethe-entropy}

where $h(v)=-v\ln v-(1-v)\ln(1-v)$. This Fermi-like combinatorics counts
Bethe quantum numbers even though the physical particles are bosons. It must
not be confused with assigning fermionic exchange statistics to the atoms.
The thermodynamic Bethe ansatz originates in @yang1969thermodynamics.

## Deriving the thermal Bethe ansatz

Equilibrium minimizes $f=e-\mu n-Ts_{\mathrm{YY}}$ while respecting
@eq-bethe-root-density. Set $\mathsf K f(k)=\int dq\,K(k-q)f(q)/(2\pi)$,
so $\delta\rho_s=\mathsf K\delta\rho_p$.
Since $\rho_h=\rho_s-\rho_p$, direct variation of the entropy gives

$$
\delta s_{\mathrm{YY}}
=\int dk\,\left[\ln\frac{\rho_h}{\rho_p}
+\mathsf K\ln\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_h}\right]\delta\rho_p.
$$

The kernel is symmetric in this model, allowing it to move between factors in
the integral. Define the dimensionless pseudoenergy
$\eta=\ln(\rho_h/\rho_p)$. Stationarity of $f$ then yields

$$
\eta(k)=\beta(k^2-\mu)-\mathsf K\ln[1+e^{-\eta}](k),
\qquad
\vartheta(k)=\frac1{1+e^{\eta(k)}}.
$$ {#eq-bethe-tba}

A pseudoenergy is a thermodynamic auxiliary function determining the filling;
it is generally not the bare energy of an isolated particle. The sequence of
a calculation is now explicit: solve @eq-bethe-tba for $\eta$, compute
$\vartheta$, solve @eq-bethe-root-density for $\rho_s$, and integrate observables.
At $c\to\infty$, $K\to0$ and $\rho_s=1/(2\pi)$: impenetrable bosons have
free-fermion thermodynamics. At very small $c$, naive numerical grids require
care because the kernel becomes narrow rather than uniformly small.

The XXZ chain has multiple quasiparticle species, including bound-state strings.
The same logic produces coupled density and pseudoenergy equations indexed by
species. Their precise kernels and string content depend on anisotropy. The
single-species derivation here supplies the logic; it does not license using the
Lieb–Liniger kernel for a spin chain.

The impenetrable limit also supplies a zero-temperature analytic benchmark.
The filling is one for $|k|<k_F$ and zero outside, with
$n=\int_{-k_F}^{k_F}dk/(2\pi)=k_F/\pi$.
Consequently $k_F=\pi n$ and
$e=\int_{-k_F}^{k_F}dk\,k^2/(2\pi)=\pi^2n^3/3$.
The edge velocity is $2k_F=2\pi n$ in the mass convention $m=1/2$.
These quantities are not evidence that the bosonic wavefunction has become a
fermionic state; local thermodynamics and density spectra share a mapping while
certain off-diagonal bosonic correlations retain different structure. Comparing
energy and sound velocity to these formulas is a more discriminating numerical
check than merely observing that a TBA iteration stopped changing.

## Dressing: how a medium changes a particle's charge

Adding a quasiparticle shifts all other roots. Its effective charge therefore
includes a response of the background. For a bare one-particle function $h(k)$,
define its *dressing* by

$$
h^{\mathrm{dr}}=h+\mathsf K(\vartheta h^{\mathrm{dr}}),
\qquad
h^{\mathrm{dr}}=(1-\mathsf K\vartheta)^{-1}h.
$$ {#eq-bethe-dressing}

The inverse means solving a linear integral equation. It is not pointwise
division. The density equation implies $2\pi\rho_s=(1)^{\mathrm{dr}}$.
The effective velocity is
$v^{\mathrm{eff}}=(2k)^{\mathrm{dr}}/(1)^{\mathrm{dr}}$ for the bare
energy $k^2$ and momentum $k$. This formula will acquire a collision-shift
interpretation in @sec-ghd.

For a numerical implementation, choose quadrature nodes $k_i$, weights $w_i$,
and matrix $M_{ij}=w_jK(k_i-k_j)\vartheta(k_j)/(2\pi)$.
Then solve $(I-M)h^{\mathrm{dr}}=h$ with a linear solver. Verify the residual,
refine the domain and grid, and recover the $c\to\infty$ result. Iterating TBA
and solving dressing are different numerical problems; convergence of one does
not certify the other.

## Why a generalized Gibbs ensemble is necessary

A maximum-entropy state constrained by conserved charges is

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{GGE}}=Z^{-1}\exp\!\left(-\sum_r\lambda_rQ_r\right).
$$ {#eq-bethe-gge}

Its multipliers reproduce the initial charge densities. Ordinary Gibbs
statistics retains energy, particle number, and other familiar global charges.
A generalized Gibbs ensemble retains enough local and quasilocal charges to
specify the locally stationary macrostate. A formally incomplete charge family
can predict the wrong steady state even when every included constraint is
satisfied.

A transparent example uses free fermions. If mode occupations are $n(k)$, then

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{GGE}}\propto e^{-\sum_k\lambda(k)c_k^\dagger c_k},
\qquad
\lambda(k)=\ln\frac{1-n(k)}{n(k)}.
$$

Take a hopping dispersion $\epsilon(k)=J\cos k$ and
$n(k)=1/2+a\cos2k$ with $|a|<1/2$. All these states have the same density
$1/2$ and energy density zero, but
$\langle c_x^\dagger c_{x+2}\rangle=a/2$.
A thermal state specified only by $n$ and $e$ cannot reproduce this continuous
family. The extra mode information affects a short-range observable, so it is
not merely inaccessible global bookkeeping.

Local stationarity after a quench follows through dephasing of oscillatory
contributions, under appropriate assumptions on the initial state and spectrum.
The global pure state remains pure. The GGE describes local measurements; it
is not the full wavefunction. Finite-size recurrences, exceptional degeneracies,
and observables with support increasing with time require separate treatment.

## Thermodynamic fluctuations contain dressed charges too

Dressing determines more than velocities. It also determines how local
conserved quantities fluctuate in a Bethe macrostate. This provides an
independent consistency check on a TBA implementation and a bridge to transport.
To see the first step, write the thermal driving term as
$w(k)=\beta k^2-\lambda$, with $\lambda=\beta\mu$.
Differentiate the pseudoenergy equation with respect to $\lambda$.
Because $d\ln(1+e^{-\eta})/d\eta=-\vartheta$, one obtains

$$
\partial_\lambda\eta=-1+\mathsf K(\vartheta\partial_\lambda\eta),
\qquad
\partial_\lambda\eta=-(1)^{\mathrm{dr}}.
$$ {#eq-bethe-pseudoenergy-response}

Thus
$\partial_\lambda\vartheta=\vartheta(1-\vartheta)(1)^{\mathrm{dr}}$.
The physical particle density is not simply the integral of filling over a fixed
density of states: $\rho_s$ changes too. Differentiating the density equation,
or equivalently moving the symmetric dressing resolvent between the two factors
in the integral, yields

$$
\chi_\lambda=\frac{\partial n}{\partial\lambda}
=\int dk\,\rho_p(k)[1-\vartheta(k)]
\left[(1)^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)\right]^2.
$$ {#eq-bethe-compressibility}

Each factor has a meaning. The occupation variance supplies
$\vartheta(1-\vartheta)$, the available-state density counts the modes, and the
dressed charge measures how a mode changes the total particle content after the
background responds. The result is nonnegative, as a susceptibility must be.
At $c\to\infty$ it reduces to
$\int dk\,\vartheta(1-\vartheta)/(2\pi)$.
For a general charge $h$, replace both unit dressed charges by $h^{\mathrm{dr}}$;
cross-correlations use one dressed factor for each charge.

A practical numerical test computes the left side by centered differences of
$n(\lambda)$ and the right side by quadrature. Agreement tests the nonlinear TBA,
the state-density equation, and the linear dressing solve simultaneously.
Choose the finite-difference step small enough to resolve a derivative but large
enough to avoid cancellation error. Grid convergence is still needed: two
methods can agree on the same inadequate rapidity cutoff.

This calculation clarifies why finite sets of charge moments can be dangerous.
Matching energy and density constrains two integrals, while response to an
additional driving function probes a whole different direction in macrostate
space. Conversely, reproducing all short-range correlators to a specified
accuracy need not require representing every mathematically possible charge
explicitly. Charge completeness is a statement about the intended class of local
states and observables, rather than a count of formal commuting matrices.

## Research bridges

The discovery of quasilocal current-overlapping charges in @prosen2011drude
explains why “I included all familiar charges” is not a completeness argument.
A first project is to examine symmetry parities of the current and candidate
charges before constructing a Mazur bound. Missing overlap can reflect a
missing symmetry sector in charge space.

@alba2017entanglement connects Bethe thermodynamics to post-quench entanglement:
the Yang–Yang entropy carried by quasiparticles enters a predictive space-time
scaling formula. Its useful starting point is a quench whose stationary root
densities are known and whose entangled quasiparticle structure fits the
construction. Arbitrary initial states and all Rényi entropies need not follow
the same simple pair formula.

The GHD papers @castro2016ghd and @bertini2016ghd turn these stationary
macrostates into locally varying fluids. This is the crucial conceptual bridge:
Bethe ansatz is more than a way to list energy levels. It supplies the local
state variables, equations of state, and velocities needed for dynamics.
The modern scope and limitations are reviewed in @doyon2025perspective.

## Exercises and selected solutions

1. Derive the two-magnon contact condition and @eq-bethe-scattering. Check
   the $\Delta=0$ limit and conservation of scattering probability for real
   nonexceptional momenta.
2. Starting from the binomial multiplicity, derive @eq-bethe-entropy including
   cancellation of the $L\ln L$ terms.
3. Vary the constrained free energy to obtain @eq-bethe-tba. Identify precisely
   where symmetry of the Lieb–Liniger kernel is used.
4. Calculate $\langle c_x^\dagger c_{x+r}\rangle$ for the free-mode example.
   Which local conserved quadratic charge detects $a$?
5. Implement a quadrature dressing solver. Compare the relative residual and
   the physical observable error as the rapidity cutoff is enlarged.
6. Design a test of a proposed finite-charge GGE against exact free-fermion
   evolution. Choose an observable absent from its fitted constraints.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution: the hidden short-range charge"}
Fourier inversion gives
$\langle c_x^\dagger c_{x+r}\rangle=
\int dk\,e^{ikr}n(k)/(2\pi)$.
The result is $1/2$ for $r=0$, $a/2$ for $r=\pm2$, and zero otherwise.
The conserved quadratic charge
$Q_2=\sum_x(c_x^\dagger c_{x+2}+c_{x+2}^\dagger c_x)$ has density $a$.
It commutes with any translationally invariant quadratic hopping Hamiltonian
because both are diagonal in $n_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution sketch: entropy counting"}
For a bin with $M=L\rho_sdk$ available states and $N=L\rho_pdk$ particles,
$\ln\binom MN\simeq M\ln M-N\ln N-(M-N)\ln(M-N)$.
Because $M=N+(M-N)$, terms proportional to $\ln(Ldk)$ cancel.
Divide by $L$, sum bins, and take the continuum limit. The remaining
integrand is exactly @eq-bethe-entropy. This derivation also explains why holes
must be counted together with particles.
:::
